title: Setting coefficients to zero
objectives: Use the lasso to select features.
Explain why the absolute-value penalty produces exact zeros, and what a zero does not mean.

screens.title: A penalty that bites
screens.prose: The same six features as last lesson, but a new penalty: $\alpha$ times the sum of the coefficients' sizes, $\sum_j |\beta_j|$. Each curve is one coefficient's size. Slide $\alpha$ and watch the curves meet the axis.
screens.question: How many coefficients are not zero at $\alpha = 0.1$?

widget.label: Coefficients not zero at alpha 0.1
widget.accept: 4: mom, value, vol and size; turnover and beta are 0.

hints.text: Set $\alpha = 0.1$ and read the caption.
Two small curves have already landed on the axis.
A coefficient is 0 once $\alpha$ passes its OLS size. Sizes 0.08 and 0.05 are below 0.1.

feedback.correct: Four survive at $\alpha = 0.1$; turnover and beta are exactly 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to 0.10 and count the curves still above the axis.

byKey.six: You expected ridge's behaviour, where nothing reaches 0. Here two curves have landed by $\alpha = 0.1$.
byKey.three: Size, at 0.12, is still above 0.1: it lands at $\alpha = 0.12$.

explain.text: Each size falls in a straight line, $|\hat\beta_j| - \alpha$, and stops at 0. Beta lands at 0.05, turnover at 0.08 and size at 0.12: the three noise features go first. Real effects survive longer simply because they are larger.

screens.title: The lasso
screens.prose: This is the **lasso**. scikit-learn's `Lasso(alpha=a)` minimises $$\frac{1}{2n}\sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2 + \alpha\sum_j |\beta_j|.$$ With features like ours, each coefficient moves $\alpha$ towards 0 and stops there. The bars show the signed coefficients.
screens.question: vol's OLS coefficient is −0.3. What is its lasso coefficient at $\alpha = 0.2$?

hints.text: Slide to 0.2 and read the vol bar.
Towards 0 means up, for a negative coefficient.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move −0.3 a distance of 0.2 towards 0.

byKey.sign: You shrank its size correctly but flipped the sign. The lasso never pushes a coefficient past 0.
byKey.away: You moved it away from 0. The penalty always pulls towards 0.
byKey.zero: Not yet: vol's size, 0.3, is more than 0.2, so it survives.

explain.text: The lasso subtracts $\alpha$ from each size and keeps the sign: $-0.3 \to -0.1$. Ridge would scale instead, and never reach 0. Here size, turnover and beta are already 0 at $\alpha = 0.2$.

screens.title: Why it stops at zero
screens.prose: With uncorrelated z-scored features, each coefficient solves its own problem: minimise $\tfrac{1}{2}(\beta - b)^2 + \alpha|\beta|$, where $b$ is the OLS value. Put the argument in order.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: If $\beta > 0$, the slope is $\beta - b + \alpha$; it is 0 at $\beta = b - \alpha$, which is positive only when $b > \alpha$
If $\beta < 0$, the slope is $\beta - b - \alpha$; it is 0 at $\beta = b + \alpha$, which is negative only when $b < -\alpha$
If $|b| \le \alpha$, neither side has a stationary point, the function falls towards 0 from both sides, so the minimum is at the kink $\beta = 0$

hints.text: $|\beta|$ has a kink at 0, so treat $\beta > 0$ and $\beta < 0$ separately.
The two sides come first, in either order; then what is left over.
Positive side, negative side, the case where neither works, then the formula.

feedback.correct: The kink at 0 is a minimum for a whole range of $b$: that is where exact zeros come from.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Handle each sign of $\beta$, then the case neither covers, then summarise.

byKey.res: The formula summarises all three cases, so it comes last.
byKey.kink: The kink case is what is left after both signs fail, so it follows them.

explain.text: A squared penalty has slope 0 at $\beta = 0$, so it never holds a coefficient there. $|\beta|$ has a corner with slopes $\pm\alpha$, and any $b$ with $|b| \le \alpha$ is held at exactly 0.

screens.title: Soft thresholding in code
screens.prose: Write the one-step lasso operator. It takes a number $z$ and a threshold $t \ge 0$, and moves $z$ a distance $t$ towards 0, stopping at 0.
screens.question: Complete `soft_threshold(z, t)`.

hints.text: A positive $z$ above the threshold loses $t$.
A negative $z$ below $-t$ gains $t$.
`return z - t` in the first branch and `return z + t` in the second.

feedback.correct: At $t = 0.1$ the six coefficients become 0.5, 0.3, −0.2, 0.02, 0 and 0.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Subtract $t$ from a large positive $z$, add $t$ to a large negative one, else return 0.

explain.text: Every lasso solver repeats this step, one coefficient at a time, on the partial residuals. With uncorrelated z-scored features one pass is the whole answer.

screens.title: Diamond against circle
screens.prose: Another view: minimise the squared errors subject to $|\beta_1| + |\beta_2| \le 1$, the shaded diamond. The ellipses are levels of the squared error, smallest at OLS. Grow them until one first touches the diamond.
screens.question: Tap the point where the growing ellipses first touch the diamond.

hints.text: The outer ellipse is the first one to reach the diamond.
Follow the outer ellipse down towards the diamond's top.
The outer ellipse just meets the corner A at $(0, 1)$, where $\beta_1 = 0$.

feedback.correct: The ellipse touches at the corner A, so $\beta_1 = 0$ exactly.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the outermost ellipse meets the diamond.

byKey.E1: B lies on an edge just inside the outer ellipse, so the squared error there is larger. The touch is at the corner.
byKey.E2: C is further from OLS. The touch is at the corner A.
byKey.C2: D is on the far side from OLS. The touch is at A.

explain.text: A diamond's corners stick out, so an ellipse usually reaches a corner first, and at a corner one coefficient is 0. The dashed circle, ridge's constraint, has no corners: it is touched at $(0.43, 0.90)$, both non-zero.

screens.title: Which features survive?
screens.prose: `Lasso(alpha=a, max_iter=10000).fit(X, y)` puts the coefficients in `.coef_`. The solver cycles through the coefficients until they settle; `max_iter=10000` gives it room on noisy data, where the default 1,000 can stop early with a warning.

state.caption: `make_panel(2)`, rows 1 to 300. Only features 0, 1 and 2 truly matter.

screens.question: Complete `lasso_support(X, y, alpha)` so it returns the sorted indices of the non-zero coefficients.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_panel(seed, n=400, p=10):
    """n share-months in month order, p features (z-scores), next-month return in %.
    Only the first three features matter: 0.6, 0.4 and -0.3 per unit."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.standard_normal((n, p))
    beta = np.zeros(p)
    beta[:3] = [0.6, 0.4, -0.3]
    y = 0.5 + X @ beta + 3.0 * rng.standard_normal(n)
    return X, y

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso

def lasso_support(X, y, alpha):
    model = Lasso(alpha=alpha, max_iter=10000).fit(X, y)
    coef = model.coef_
    return [int(i) for i in np.flatnonzero(coef)]

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_panel(seed, n=400, p=10):
    """n share-months in month order, p features (z-scores), next-month return in %.
    Only the first three features matter: 0.6, 0.4 and -0.3 per unit."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.standard_normal((n, p))
    beta = np.zeros(p)
    beta[:3] = [0.6, 0.4, -0.3]
    y = 0.5 + X @ beta + 3.0 * rng.standard_normal(n)
    return X, y

screens.title: Zero is not no effect
screens.prose: Two momentum signals, 6-month and 12-month, have correlation 0.97. In this generated market each truly adds 0.3% per unit. A colleague fits the lasso at $\alpha = 0.1$ on 300 share-months.
screens.question: The colleague writes: 6-month momentum has no effect on returns. What is the right reading?

options.text: The two signals carry nearly the same information, and the lasso kept one of them; mom6 may matter as much as mom12
Agreed: the lasso tested mom6 and found no effect
options.why: You read a zero as a test result. The lasso keeps the cheaper of two near-copies; that is a choice, not a test.

options.text: mom12 is the true signal and mom6 a weaker copy of it
options.why: You trusted which one survived. On another sample from the same market the lasso kept mom6 and dropped mom12.

options.text: Trust OLS instead: mom6 is worth 0.05 and mom12 0.44
options.why: OLS splits correlated signals noisily; both of its numbers are far from the true 0.30.

hints.text: What does a correlation of 0.97 say about the two columns?
Compare the true row with the lasso row.
With near-copies, one coefficient can do the work of both, and the penalty charges less for one large coefficient than for two.

feedback.correct: A lasso zero means not needed alongside the others, not no effect.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what the lasso does with two near-identical columns.

byKey.noeffect: You read the zero as evidence of no effect. With a near-copy in the model, the lasso can drop either one.

explain.text: The lasso put 0.38 on mom12 and 0 on mom6, while the truth is 0.30 each. On another sample (seed 9) it kept mom6 at 0.44 and zeroed mom12. Ridge would share the weight between them instead.

screens.title: The far end
screens.prose: Back to the six uncorrelated features. As $\alpha$ grows, coefficients leave one by one until none is left and the model forecasts the training mean.
screens.question: What is the smallest $\alpha$ at which every coefficient is 0?

widget.label: Smallest alpha with every coefficient zero

hints.text: Which curve reaches the axis last?
mom has the largest OLS size.
mom's size is 0.6, so it reaches 0 at $\alpha = 0.6$.

feedback.correct: At $\alpha = 0.6$ the last coefficient, mom, reaches 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the last curve meets the axis.

byKey.inf: That is ridge's far end. The lasso empties the model at a finite $\alpha$.
byKey.sum: You added the sizes. The model is empty once $\alpha$ passes the largest one.
byKey.small: That is where the first coefficient leaves, not the last.

explain.text: Every coefficient is 0 once $\alpha \ge \max_j |b_j| = 0.6$, and the forecast is the training mean. In general that point is $\alpha_{\max} = \max_j |\mathbf{x}_j^T(\mathbf{y} - \bar y)| / n$ for centred columns. Solvers start their grid there and walk down.

screens.title: The lasso, and its units
screens.prose: Textbooks write the lasso as $\sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2 + \lambda\sum_j |\beta_j|$. scikit-learn divides the first term by $2n$, so $$\lambda = 2n\alpha.$$ `Ridge(alpha)` uses no such factor. The **elastic net** mixes both penalties: it zeroes coefficients but shares weight across correlated features.
screens.question: A lasso on $n = 200$ rows uses `Lasso(alpha=0.1)`. What is the textbook $\lambda$?

options.why: You multiplied by $n$ only. The $\tfrac{1}{2n}$ in front of the squared errors makes the factor $2n$.
You assumed the conventions match. They differ by $2n$.
You divided by $2n$. Multiply both sides of scikit-learn's objective by $2n$ instead.

hints.text: Multiply scikit-learn's objective by $2n$.
The squared errors lose their $\tfrac{1}{2n}$; the penalty becomes $2n\alpha\sum|\beta_j|$.
$2 \times 200 \times 0.1 = 40$.

explain.text: Multiplying an objective by a constant does not move its minimum, so both forms give the same coefficients when $\lambda = 2n\alpha$. Check the convention before copying a penalty from a paper.

screens.title: Two hundred candidate signals
screens.prose: A desk screens 200 candidate signals on 240 months of a strategy's returns. At $\alpha = 0.53$ the lasso keeps 5. Refitted by OLS they explain 9.8% of the 240 months. We generated all 200 as pure noise.
screens.question: If each of 200 pure-noise signals were tested on its own at the 5% level, how many would you expect to pass?

hints.text: Each noise signal passes a 5% test with probability 0.05.
Expected passes add up across the 200 tests.

feedback.correct: Ten false discoveries are expected from noise alone.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the number of tests by the false-positive rate.

byKey.zero: You expected noise never to pass. At 5%, one in twenty does by chance.
byKey.five: That is the 5% read as a count. It is a rate: 5% of 200.
byKey.one: One would be the expected count for 20 tests, not 200.

explain.text: Searching 200 signals guarantees survivors, as the `testing` course's multiple-testing lesson showed. These five scored -13.9% on the next 120 months. A desk wants an economic reason, a much stricter threshold, and fresh data before trading any of them.

ideas: The lasso penalises $\sum_j |\beta_j|$; coefficients move towards 0 and stop there, one by one, so it selects features.
The corner of $|\beta|$ at 0, like the diamond's corners, is what makes exact zeros; ridge's smooth penalty never does.
A zero means not needed alongside the others: with correlated features the lasso keeps one, and searches over many signals keep some noise.
summary.trap: A zeroed coefficient does not mean no effect: of two correlated signals the lasso keeps one, and which one can change with the sample.

quiz.prose: A colleague chooses the lasso's $\alpha$ by the lowest training MSE.
quiz.question: Which $\alpha$ will they pick?

options.text: The smallest on the grid, the one closest to OLS
One in the middle, where bias and variance balance
options.why: That balance shows only on held-out rows. On training rows less penalty always fits better.

options.text: The largest, because it keeps the fewest features
options.why: Fewer features fit the training rows worse, not better.
On training rows it does not: the penalty only ever raises training error.

feedback.correct: The penalty can only cost training fit, so training MSE always prefers none.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the penalty does to the fit on the rows it was fitted to.

explain.text: Any penalty moves the coefficients away from the training least squares solution, so training MSE rises with $\alpha$. Choosing by training error always picks $\alpha \approx 0$.

quiz.prose: A dataset contains the same column twice, $x_3$ and an exact copy $x_4$, both useful.
quiz.question: What do ridge and the lasso do with the pair?

options.text: Ridge splits the weight equally; the lasso can put it all on one copy

options.why: Splitting costs the lasso nothing extra, but nothing makes it split; scikit-learn's solver gives it all to the first copy it updates.

options.text: Both put it all on one copy
options.why: For ridge, $c^2/2 + c^2/2 < c^2$, so splitting is strictly cheaper.
Penalised fits have an answer even with duplicate columns; for ridge it is unique.

feedback.correct: Squares reward sharing; absolute values are indifferent to it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the penalties of $(c, 0)$ and $(c/2, c/2)$.

explain.text: Ridge: $c^2 > 2(c/2)^2$, so it shares. Lasso: $|c| = |c/2| + |c/2|$, so any split costs the same, and the solver usually leaves one copy at 0.

quiz.prose: Uncorrelated z-scored features. A coefficient's OLS value is $-0.45$.
quiz.question: What is its lasso value at $\alpha = 0.3$?

byKey.sign: You dropped the sign. Soft thresholding keeps it.
byKey.zero: Its size, 0.45, is above 0.3, so it survives.
